title: India's Cockroach Movement Wins First Government Meeting After Tear Gas and Baton Charges Near Parliament
excerpt: Health Minister JP Nadda agreed to meet CJP leaders as police fired tear gas at 10,000 protesters marching on Parliament during the Monsoon session's opening day.
body:
• Police fired tear gas and baton-charged an estimated 10,000 Cockroach Janta Party protesters attempting to march from Jantar Mantar to Parliament on Monday, the first day of the Monsoon session.
  • Health Minister JP Nadda agreed to meet CJP spokesperson Saurav Das, marking the Modi government's first direct engagement with the movement's leadership.
  • The protests intensified after police forcibly moved hunger-striking activist Sonam Wangchuk to hospital on Saturday; CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke has since taken up the fast.
  • The CJP demands Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation over NEET 2026 paper leaks that forced two million students to resit exams and drove at least a dozen to suicide.

Police fired tear gas and charged protesters with batons on Monday as thousands of India's Cockroach Janta Party supporters tried to breach security barricades and march on Parliament in New Delhi, turning the opening day of the Monsoon session into a test of the government's willingness to face down its most sustained youth-led challenge.

An estimated 10,000 demonstrators had massed at Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site about two kilometres from Parliament, by Monday morning, according to Delhi's Deputy Commissioner of Police Sachin Sharma. The crowd included students, professionals and families with young children who had arrived through the night after police forcibly moved hunger-striking activist Sonam Wangchuk to hospital on Saturday — a decision that galvanised the movement.

Clashes and Denials

Television visuals showed police caning protesters in a heavily barricaded area near Parliament. Reuters journalists in the area reported hearing blasts, and the CJP said tear gas had been fired to disperse demonstrators, though Delhi Police denied any use of force, insisting the "protest is being handled professionally."

Government offices in the Parliament area were locked to prevent protesters from entering. The CJP had announced the "Chalo Sansad" march despite police denying permission, invoking Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita Suraksha — the replacement for the old Section 144 — which bars gatherings of five or more people outside Jantar Mantar without prior approval.

""We shall win!" Das wrote on X after confirming the meeting.</p> <p>The dual approach of force and dialogue reflects the government's dilemma."

"All these leaders in power are illiterate and I am here to protest because we do not want question papers to leak. This should come to an end."

— Adi Nathan, 21, student from Meerut

A Shift in Tone

Even as police swung batons, the Modi government appeared to shift its position. Health Minister JP Nadda agreed to meet CJP spokesperson Saurav Das — the first direct engagement between the government and the movement's leadership since protests began in late May. "We shall win!" Das wrote on X after confirming the meeting.

The dual approach of force and dialogue reflects the government's dilemma. Senior leaders, including Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, have accused protesters of acting against the nation. But with millions of followers on social media and growing sympathy across opposition parties, the Cockroach movement has become a political force that cannot be easily dismissed.

From Insult to Movement

The CJP emerged in May after India's Chief Justice compared some unemployed young people to "cockroaches" during an unrelated hearing. Supporters embraced the slur, turning it into a satirical identity that has resonated with a generation frustrated by exam fraud, limited government jobs and rising youth unemployment.

The immediate trigger was the leak of NEET 2026 medical entrance exam papers, which affected more than two million students and forced them to sit the test a second time. At least a dozen students died by suicide in the aftermath. The movement's demands include Pradhan's resignation, systemic reform of the examination system and compensation for families of students who died.

What the Diaspora Is Watching

The protests have drawn attention from Indian communities abroad, many of whom went through India's competitive exam system before emigrating. The integrity of entrance exams for engineering, medical and civil service posts has long been a concern for NRI families with children studying in India or considering returning. The NEET leaks touched a nerve across the diaspora, where exam preparation often begins years before the test date.

What Happens Next

CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke has taken up the hunger strike after Wangchuk's hospitalisation, and the movement has vowed to continue protests throughout the Monsoon session. Opposition parties have signalled they will raise the NEET crisis in Parliament, ensuring the issue stays in the national spotlight. Wangchuk, who has set conditions for ending his fast — including government accountability for educational failures or assurances from MPs — remains in hospital under restricted movement.

The outcome of the Nadda-Das meeting will be closely watched. If the government offers concrete steps toward exam reform, it could defuse weeks of tension. If the talks amount to little more than optics, the CJP's next march may draw even larger crowds.
